title: What you actually need to install, and what you don't
promise: You're going to end up with the exact minimum list to get started: five things, four of them free accounts and zero installations. And you'll be able to recognize the four signs that tell you it's genuinely time to install something.
why: Rubén is 41 and a physical therapist in Gijón. He wanted a website where his patients could book appointments without calling his cell. One Saturday morning he pulled up a video titled "Build your website with AI in 20 minutes." The first fourteen minutes of the video were installing programs. An hour and a half later he had four new things on his laptop and zero web pages. He also had a black window with a red error he didn't understand. He closed the computer and didn't open it again for three months. When he picked it back up, he built the whole website in one afternoon, without installing a single thing. The only thing he downloaded in the whole process was his own logo file.

theory.title: Installing isn't starting. It's one of the last things you do
theory.text: Installing means copying a program into your computer so it lives there. It's not an innocent step. Every installed program takes up disk space and updates itself every few weeks. Sometimes it asks for the admin password. And every once in a while it clashes with something else you had. So every install is a small debt you pay off later. You pay it the day something stops working and you don't know which of the six things you installed is to blame. Tutorials start there because they're written by people who code and who've already had all of that set up for years. For them, installing is opening a door that's already open. For you it's a forty-minute wall before you've seen anything of your own on screen, and that's where most people give up. The right question isn't "what do I need to install." It's "what's the first thing I want to see working." And then, only if needed, "what am I missing to see it." You'll install things someday. But you'll install them when you hit a specific, named wall, not because a video tells you to at minute three.
theory.analogy: It's like signing up for the gym and spending the first month buying shoes, leggings, a fitness tracker, a blender, and supplements. By the time you finally get to the treadmill you're already exhausted, you've spent $200, and you still haven't run a single minute.
theory.example: Rubén's video told him to install Node.js, Git, Visual Studio Code, and two extensions before writing a single line. Between downloads, restarts, and one wrongly checked box, ninety minutes were gone. The website he ended up building three months later didn't use any of those four things.

theory.title: The two places your project can live
theory.text: Your project can live in two places, and understanding the difference saves you half the headaches. One is the cloud: other companies' computers that you use from your browser without installing anything. It's just like writing a document in Google Docs without having installed Word. The other is local, meaning inside your own computer, with files in a folder and programs that run them. Almost everything you'll do the first few months fits entirely in the cloud. The AI writes the code and shows it to you already working, in a panel next to the conversation. GitHub stores the files and also lets you edit them from its website. Vercel takes what's in GitHub and publishes it on the internet with its own address. None of those three things needs you to install anything. What the cloud doesn't give you is getting your hands into your own files. Imagine you have 300 PDF invoices in a folder on your disk and need to process them in a batch. Or you want a program running on your machine twenty-four hours a day. That's when you go local. The doubt that'll come up is whether working this way is some toy version, and it isn't. A business website with text, photos, a contact form, and appointment booking gets built entirely in the browser. And it ends up just as published as any other.
theory.analogy: The cloud is renting an industrial kitchen by the hour: you go in, cook, and leave, without buying the oven. Local is setting up the kitchen in your own house: you can do whatever you want whenever you want. But first there's construction, installation, and bills.
theory.example: Rubén's website is three pages, an appointment form that emails him, and a map. It's published at an address ending in .vercel.app and costs $0 a month. He built it without installing a single program. The only thing he paid for was the domain rubenfisio.com: $12 a year.

theory.title: The real minimum list: five things, and four are accounts
theory.text: This is everything you need to start today, and there's no fine print. First, an updated browser: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari. You already have it. Second, an account with one of the three AIs (ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini). It can be free, or about $20 a month if you're going seriously. Third, a GitHub account, which is where your project's files get saved along with their change history. It costs $0 and doesn't ask for a card. Fourth, a Vercel account, the company that takes what's in GitHub and puts it on the internet. Its starter plan, called Hobby, also costs $0 and doesn't ask for a card either. And fifth, a folder on your desktop with two or three text files where you keep track of the project's state and your prompts. A prompt is the instruction you write for the AI. You write those files with Windows Notepad or Mac TextEdit, which already come installed. Total: four accounts, zero new programs on your computer, and between $0 and $20 a month. The only thing that might get added later is your own domain, $5 to $15 a year.
theory.example: Rubén, day one: updated Chrome ($0), Claude Pro ($20/month, which he already paid for), GitHub account with username ruben-fisio ($0), Vercel account signing in with the GitHub button ($0), and a folder called my-website on the desktop with three text files inside. Ten minutes of setup, and after that all the time went into the website, not the setup.

theory.title: What you do NOT need yet, and why they'll recommend it to you anyway
theory.text: This is the list of what you can safely leave for later, with the real reason for each. Node.js is the engine that runs code meant for websites on your own computer. You'll need it the day you want to see your website working on your machine before publishing it, not a minute before. Python is the same, but for processing data and files in batches. So it shows up once you have your own files to chew through. You don't need Git typed into a terminal either. GitHub has its website and also a windows-and-buttons program called GitHub Desktop, which does the same thing without typing commands. The terminal is that black window where you type instructions. You won't need it, except to paste the occasional loose command the AI gives you. And that's not learning the terminal, that's pasting a sentence. Docker packages a program with everything it needs so it works the same on any computer. It takes up several gigs and reserves memory even when you're not using it. It's for when you work with more people or with servers. Models that run on your own machine, like Ollama or LM Studio, take up 4 to 5 GB per model. They want 16 GB of memory to run decently. And even then they give you a result well below the app you're already using for free. An API key is the password a program of yours uses to talk to the AI. You only need it the day your project has to talk to the AI without you in front of it. And buying a domain before having a website is paying for a sign with no shop behind it. They'll recommend all of it to you anyway, the AI included. Its default answer is one programmer talking to another. It stops doing that as soon as you tell it who you are.
theory.example: In the second message, Claude suggested to Rubén "install Node.js and run npm create vite." Rubén replied with just one sentence: "I don't know how to use the terminal and I'd rather not install anything yet, can this be done just in the browser?" The next answer was already a complete page working in the side panel, nothing installed.

theory.title: The wall: the four signs it's genuinely time to install
theory.text: Don't install out of caution. Install when you hit a wall. Sign one: you want to see your website working on your computer, with every change reflected instantly and without publishing every test to the internet. That's Node.js, and it usually shows up once the project grows from one page to several. Sign two: you have your own files on disk and need to process them in a batch. For example, 300 invoice PDFs, a 12,000-row Excel sheet, or 800 photos that need resizing. That's Python. Sign three: your project already has more than fifteen files. Editing them one by one on the GitHub website has become a click-fest. That's GitHub Desktop and Visual Studio Code. Visual Studio Code is a code editor, meaning a Notepad with superpowers that colors the text and warns you about mistakes. Sign four: you need something to happen every day at 8:00 with nobody watching. That doesn't get installed on your computer, it gets hosted in the cloud, because your laptop is off inside a bag at that hour. The order is always the same: browser, AI account, GitHub, and Vercel. And only after hitting a wall: GitHub Desktop, Visual Studio Code, Node.js, and Python. Install one thing per wall and never two at once. That way, when something breaks, you'll know exactly what broke it.
theory.analogy: You don't buy a ten-foot ladder because someday you'll need to change a light bulb. You buy it the day the bulb is burned out and you can't reach it.
theory.example: Rubén hit wall number one after six weeks. His website had five pages and publishing every test to the internet just to see it was taking forever. He installed Node.js from nodejs.org, LTS version, 78 MB, eight minutes. It was the first and only thing he installed in four months of the project.

theory.title: Installing without messing up, and the cheat sheet that prevents half the problems
theory.text: When the day comes, just four rules. First: always download from the official website and only from there. The official ones are nodejs.org, python.org, code.visualstudio.com, desktop.github.com, and git-scm.com. Never download from a video's link, a forum, or the first sponsored search result. There are copies with almost identical names that serve the real program with a gift inside, and that damage doesn't undo by uninstalling. Second: always pick the version marked LTS, which means long-term support. The newest one breaks things and doesn't give you anything you need. Third: on Windows, leave the "Add to PATH" box checked and uncheck the extras like additional tools. On Mac, drag the program to the Applications folder and that's it. Fourth: uninstalling is possible and doesn't break anything. On Windows it's done from Settings and Apps; on Mac, by dragging to the trash. There's one exception, and you'll see it in the tasks. And apart from all that, what'll save you the most trouble isn't an installation rule. It's pasting the AI five lines telling it what computer you have. Without that it'll give you Mac instructions while you're on Windows. It'll tell you to type into a terminal you don't know how to open. And it'll talk about menus that are named differently on your screen.
theory.example: Rubén lost a whole afternoon. Claude kept giving him commands starting with brew, which only exist on Mac, while he was on Windows 11. Once he pasted five lines at the start of the chat — "Windows 11 Home, 16 GB memory, Chrome, never coded, don't know how to use the terminal" — it never happened again for the rest of the project.

tasks.title: Check the one thing you truly need today: an up-to-date browser
tasks.where: In your browser: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari
tasks.action: In Chrome, click the three vertical dots top right, go into "Help" then "About Google Chrome." That screen checks for updates on its own the moment you open it. If a blue "Relaunch" button shows up, click it and let it restart. In Edge the path is three dots, "Help and feedback," "About Microsoft Edge." Safari updates with the system: Apple menu, "System Settings," "General," "Software Update." Write down the version number it shows, for example 139.0.7258.67.
tasks.expect: A message like "Google Chrome is up to date" with a version number underneath. If it asked you to restart and you did, going back into that same screen should now say it's current.
tasks.stuck: If the update button is grayed out and mentions the administrator, you're on a work computer with limited permissions. Install Firefox from firefox.com, which will let you, or use your home computer. This matters because the panels where AI shows you the working website fail on three-year-old browsers. And then it looks like the AI's fault.

tasks.title: Write your computer's specs and paste them to the AI
tasks.where: In Windows Settings or the Mac Apple menu, and then in your AI's text box
tasks.action: On Windows 11: Start button, "Settings," "System," and at the very bottom "About." Note three things. What's listed under "Edition," for example Windows 11 Home. What's listed under "Installed RAM," for example 16.0 GB. And what's listed under "System type," almost always 64-bit. On Mac: the Apple menu top left and "About This Mac." Note the system name (for example macOS Sequoia), the chip (M2, M3, or Intel), and the memory. Open Notepad on Windows or TextEdit on Mac and write those lines down. Save the file as COMPUTER.txt on the Desktop. And from now on paste that text at the start of every new project conversation.
tasks.prompt:
Before we start I want you to know what I'm working with, and I want you to keep it in mind in ALL your answers in this chat.

My computer:
- Computer: [Windows 11 Home / MacBook Air with M2 chip and macOS Sequoia]
- Memory: [16 GB]
- Browser: [Chrome, up to date]
- Programming tools installed: [none]
- Level: I've never coded, I don't know how to use the terminal, and I'd rather not open it.

Rules for this whole chat:
1. Don't assume I have anything installed. If something's needed, tell me before using it.
2. If the solution you're thinking of needs an install, stop and tell me first whether there's a way to get the same result just in the browser, even if it's slower.
3. When giving me menu instructions, use the exact names that show up on my system, not another one.
4. Never give me a macOS command if I'm on Windows, or vice versa. If you're not sure, ask me.
5. Whenever you tell me to download something, always give me the full official web address.

Confirm in two lines that you understood, and don't do anything else yet.
tasks.expect: A COMPUTER.txt file on your desktop with five lines, and a short AI reply confirming the rules without jumping into solving anything. If it's already thrown a wall of instructions at you, it didn't read the last line, and it's worth repeating that to it.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find that info screen, take a screenshot of whatever's in front of you. On Windows that's the Windows key plus Shift plus S; on Mac, Cmd plus Shift plus 4. Upload it to the AI and ask "what computer and version do I have based on this screenshot?" Check what it tells you against the screen yourself, don't just take its word for it.

tasks.title: See what you already have installed, without opening the terminal
tasks.where: In Windows Settings, or the Mac Applications folder
tasks.action: On Windows 11: Start, "Settings," "Apps," "Installed apps." There's a search box above that same list. Type these words one at a time and write down what shows up with its version number: node, python, git, docker, code, ollama. On Mac: open Finder, go into "Applications" in the sidebar, and search the same words in the magnifying glass top right. It's normal for almost nothing to show up, and that's exactly what you want.
tasks.prompt:
I'm giving you the list of what I found installed on my computer related to programming. My system is [Windows 11 Home / macOS Sequoia].

[paste what you wrote down here, with the versions; if you found nothing, write: I found none]

Tell me, in three sections and with no jargon:
1. Which of these works as-is to build a simple website with you, with nothing else installed.
2. Which is old but doesn't matter because I won't be using it for now.
3. Which I should NEVER uninstall because the system itself or some program of mine uses it.

If the list is empty, tell me clearly and confirm what I can still do without installing anything. Don't recommend installing anything in this answer.
tasks.expect: A short list, probably empty or with one or two things. Being empty is good news: it means your computer is clean and you're starting with no strange leftovers that could get in the way later.
tasks.stuck: If something you don't remember installing shows up, like a Python 3.9 from years ago, don't uninstall it. Macs ship with a system Python and removing it breaks things on the computer; on Windows it might belong to another program of yours. Note it and move on: having something old installed doesn't get in the way of anything you're going to do.

tasks.title: Do the ten-minute test: something real without installing anything
tasks.where: In the Claude app (claude.ai) or ChatGPT (chatgpt.com), in the usual text box
tasks.action: Open a new conversation and paste the prompt below. Swap what's in brackets for your real idea, with your real details: your name, your city, your prices. Sending it will open a panel on the right side of the screen with the page already working. That panel is called Artifact in Claude, Canvas in ChatGPT, and also Canvas in Gemini. Click inside the panel, try the buttons, see if the form responds. Changes get asked for by typing in the conversation, not by touching the panel.
tasks.prompt:
I want to check one thing before I get into anything: how far we can get without installing absolutely anything on my computer.

Build me a single-screen web page for this: [describe your idea in two sentences, with real details: what it is, who it's for, what city, what you want people to do when they land on it].

Requirements:
- A headline, a sentence explaining what I offer, three content blocks, and one main button.
- Real text written by you based on what I told you, no filler like "lorem ipsum."
- Looks good on mobile.
- All in a single HTML file, with the styles and code inside the same file, with no external dependencies, so it works as-is even if I have nothing installed.

Show it to me working in the side panel. Don't explain the code or walk me through it line by line.

Once I have it in front of me, tell me in three lines and plain English: what part of my full idea CAN'T be done this way, and exactly what that part would require.
tasks.expect: A page working in the right-hand panel in under a minute, with your name and your text inside. Below it, three honest lines telling you what's left out. That moment is the proof that the installation list wasn't needed.
tasks.stuck: If no side panel shows up, reply: "Show it to me as an artifact or in canvas, not as text." If your free plan doesn't allow that today, ask for the full code and copy it. Paste it into Notepad and save it to the desktop as test.html, choosing "All files" in the type dropdown. Double-clicking it opens it in your browser and it works just as well.

tasks.title: Create your free GitHub account
tasks.action: Go to github.com and click "Sign up" top right. It asks for email, password, and username. Think through the username carefully. It's lowercase, no spaces or accents, and it shows up in the public address of all your projects. So pick something you'd show a client, like ruben-fisio, and not something like xXruben97Xx. Then it asks you to solve a small verification puzzle and enter a six-digit code sent to your email. When it asks about the plan, pick "Free." It never asks for a card.
tasks.expect: Your profile page open at github.com/your-username, with your name at the top and a notice that you don't have any repositories yet, which is what GitHub calls a project's folder. That's normal on day one and gets fixed in the next lesson.
tasks.stuck: If it takes you to a screen with $4 and $21-a-month plans, scroll all the way down and look for the "Free" column. It's always there, even if it's not the most visible. If the code doesn't arrive, check spam before requesting it again. And watch out for one thing: changing your username later breaks every link you've shared. Decide it now, not later.

tasks.title: Set up your project folder on the desktop
tasks.where: On your computer's Desktop, with Notepad or TextEdit
tasks.action: Create a new folder on the desktop and call it my-project, all lowercase, no spaces, no accents, no special characters. This isn't just fussiness: spaces and accents in folder names cause weird problems later, and avoiding them now costs nothing. Put three text files inside called exactly STATE.txt, PROMPTS.txt, and COMPUTER.txt, the last one being the one you made in task two. Use the prompt below to have the AI fill in the first one, then copy and paste it in.
tasks.prompt:
I'm going to keep a text file called STATE.txt where I track where my project stands, so I can paste it to you at the start of every new conversation and you don't have to ask me the same things every time.

My project is: [describe it in three sentences, with real details].

Write me that file's starting contents. Requirements:
- Plain text, no formatting, ready to copy and paste into Notepad.
- Maximum 25 lines.
- With these sections: what I'm building, who for, what's done, what's missing, decisions already made that I don't want revisited, accounts and addresses I already have, and what's next.
- For sections you don't know how to fill in yet, leave "pending" written instead of making anything up.
- No emojis or decoration.

After giving it to me, tell me in two sentences when I should update it and what happens if I don't.
tasks.expect: A my-project folder on your desktop with three .txt files inside, and STATE.txt with its sections written out even if half say "pending." With that, you can open a new conversation any day without losing track of what you've done.
tasks.stuck: If saving leaves you with a file called STATE.txt.txt, that's because Windows is hiding extensions. In Notepad use "File," "Save as," and in the "Type" dropdown pick "All files" before typing the name. If it's already happened, rename it by hand removing the extra .txt.

tasks.title: Learn to stop the AI when it tells you to install
tasks.where: In any AI conversation, the moment you see the word "install"
tasks.action: This isn't a one-time task, it's a reflex I want you to build today. Next time the AI tells you to install something, don't just obey. Copy and paste the text below, swapping in the name of whatever it asked for. Save it in your PROMPTS.txt to have it handy, because you'll use it ten times over the next few months.
tasks.prompt:
Hold on. Before installing anything I want to understand the decision.

Answer me in this order, no code and no steps yet:

1. What exactly is [name of what you told me to install], explained in two sentences with no technical words.
2. What specific problem in MY project does it solve. If the honest answer is "it's just standard" or "everyone uses it," say so plainly.
3. Is there any way to get today's same result without installing anything, working just in the browser? If there is, even if it's slower or uglier, I want to see that first.
4. If there truly is no alternative: how much disk space it takes, how much it costs in dollars, the exact official web address to download it from, and whether it can be uninstalled later without breaking anything.
5. What happens if I DON'T install it: what specific part of my project stays undone.

And a rule for the rest of the chat: don't give me another installation step without having answered these five questions first.
tasks.expect: Eight times out of ten an alternative that works in the browser shows up and you skip the whole install. The two times it's genuinely needed, you'll get the official address, the size, and the specific reason. Then you install calmly, knowing why.
tasks.stuck: If it insists it's "the standard" or "best practice," reply: "Standard isn't a reason. Tell me the specific result in my project I can't get without it, in one sentence." If it can't answer that, don't install it.

tasks.title: Ask for your install plan by signal, not by date
tasks.where: In your AI app, in a new conversation, with COMPUTER.txt pasted at the top
tasks.action: Open a new conversation, paste the contents of your COMPUTER.txt first, then this prompt with your real idea inside. What it gives back is your personal map. It'll tell you what you're going to have to install for your project. And it'll tell you the exact signal that'll warn you the moment has arrived. Save that table inside STATE.txt.
tasks.prompt:
This is my idea: [describe it in four sentences: what it does, who for, how many people a month will use it, and whether it has to work when I'm not around].

I work inside this app by typing in the text box. The terminal scares me and I'd rather not use it unless there's no alternative.

Make me a table with four columns: what to install, what specific signal will tell me the moment has arrived (not a date, an observable signal like "once your website grows past X"), how much disk space it takes, and what happens if I never install it.

Rules:
- Order the table by when it'll be needed, soonest to latest.
- Before the table, write one line with everything that can be done with just free accounts in the browser, labeled "0 installs."
- If my whole idea can be done without installing anything, tell me in the first line and leave the table with zero rows. Don't make up rows to look thorough.
- Don't include anything for best practices, just in case, or professionalism. Only what's needed for my idea to work and be published on the internet.

End with a single sentence: what's the FIRST thing I'm going to have to install, and what exact signal is going to trigger it.
tasks.expect: A short table, zero to four rows. Most commonly the first thing is Node.js and it arrives much later than you were afraid of. It could also turn out that nothing's needed for the version you want to publish.
tasks.stuck: If it gives you back twelve rows with Docker, Postgres, Redis, and three other things, reply: "You've made the list for a company's tech team. Redo it for one person alone, with no prior knowledge, with [N] visits a month, and remove everything that's just in case." The second version usually ends up at two rows.

tasks.title: Bookmark the five official addresses
tasks.where: In your browser, in the bookmarks bar
tasks.action: Create a bookmarks folder called "Install (official)." Put these five addresses inside, typing them yourself in the address bar: nodejs.org, python.org, code.visualstudio.com, desktop.github.com, and git-scm.com. The day you install something, go in from that folder and only from that folder. Never from a video's description link, a forum message, or the first sponsored search result.
tasks.expect: A folder in your bookmarks with five links inside, and the feeling of having done something boring. It is, and that's the point: the day you need it, you won't be rushing to decide which of six results is the real one.
tasks.stuck: To save the page you're on, press Ctrl plus D on Windows or Cmd plus D on Mac and pick the folder from the dropdown. If you don't know how to create the folder, in Chrome it's under three dots, "Bookmarks and lists," "Bookmark manager," then right-click, "Add folder." The specific reason not to skip this: there are websites with names nearly identical to the official ones. They serve the real installer with an add-on that steals passwords saved in your browser, and uninstalling it afterward doesn't give them back.

matters: Installing ahead of time is the number one cause of quitting. Nobody abandons a project because the AI writes bad code. They abandon it the Saturday ninety minutes vanish into downloads and red errors, without having seen a single screen of their own. Start with what's visible and you stick around; start with the setup and you fall in the lobby.

Download only from the official website, and type the address yourself. Copies with nearly identical names exist and serve the real program with something added inside. That add-on goes after the passwords your browser has saved. Uninstalling it afterward doesn't undo the theft: you have to change passwords one by one.

Tell the AI what computer you have, in five lines, at the start of every project conversation. Without that it'll give you Mac instructions on Windows, and menus named differently than on your screen. And you'll think you're the clumsy one. Five lines pasted at the top save whole afternoons.

Install one thing per wall and never two at once. Put in four programs the same afternoon and something stops working, you won't know which of the four broke it. You end up uninstalling blind. One at a time, with its reason written in STATE.txt, and you always know how to go back.
ignore: Version numbers and arguments about which is better. Node 20 versus 22, Python 3.11 versus 3.13: when it's your turn, grab whichever says LTS and move on. You won't notice the difference between those versions in anything you do this year.

Virtual environments and version managers, anything that sounds like juggling several installs at once: venv, conda, nvm, pyenv. They solve the problem of having fifteen different projects coexisting on one computer, and you're going to have one. They exist and will make sense someday, but not today.

AI-integrated editors like Cursor, Windsurf, or Copilot, and tools that work inside the terminal. They're great accelerators for someone who already knows where they're headed, and noise for someone still deciding what to build. You'll look at them again once your project has thirty files and you know why you want them.
canDo: Give you install steps with the real button and menu names for your system, if you've told it which one you have. With your computer's specs pasted at the top, the instructions fit on the first try. It won't send you to a menu that doesn't exist on your screen.

Build and show you complete working websites right inside the app, in the side panel, with nothing installed. A page with text, images, buttons, and a form comes out in under a minute and can be interacted with right there.

Translate any red error from a black window into plain English and tell you exactly what's missing. Paste in the error text as-is, not understanding a word of it, and it hands back "it can't find such-and-such, fix it by doing this."

Look at the list of programs you already have installed and tell you which one works for you, which one's old but doesn't matter, and which one you shouldn't touch. Paste in what you see on the Apps screen and it'll sort it for you.
cantDo: See your screen or know what you have installed. If you don't tell it or send a screenshot, it imagines it. And what it imagines is a programmer's computer with everything already set up for years.

Install anything for you. The clicks, the downloads, and the admin password are all on you. And watch out: if something asks for a password during an install, it's your computer asking, never type it inside the chat.

Know what today's version of a program is or whether its download page has changed. Its information has an expiration date; the official site doesn't. That's why you're the one who opens the address and reads what's there.

Guess at problems with your computer you haven't told it about. For example: an antivirus blocking the download, limited permissions on a work machine, a full disk, or a folder with accented characters in the name. If something fails and doesn't add up, tell it the odd detail before going in circles twenty times.
words: Install
Copying a program into your computer so it stays there and you can use it whenever. It takes up space, updates every few weeks, and can be removed later.
Local
Inside your own computer, in your own folders, only you can see it. The opposite of having it on the internet.
The cloud
Other companies' computers that you use from the browser without downloading anything. Writing a document in Google Docs without having Word installed is exactly that.
Terminal
A black window where you type commands with the keyboard instead of clicking buttons. It's intimidating at first, but for what you're doing there's almost always a button-based way to do it.
Code editor
A Notepad with superpowers: it colors the text so it reads better and warns you when something's written wrong. The most used one is called Visual Studio Code and it's free.
Node.js
The engine that runs code meant for web pages on your own computer. It's for seeing your website before you've published it.
Python
A widely used language for handling piles of files and data at once. Needed when you have your own stuff saved on disk that has to be processed in a batch.
Docker
A box that packages a program with everything it needs, so it works the same on any computer. It takes up several gigs and reserves memory even when idle.
Dependency
A piece of program made by other people that yours needs to rely on to work. If it's missing or changes, your project stops starting.
LTS version
The version of a program its authors commit to maintaining for years. It's the boring, stable one, and it's always what you want.
